Gnosticism is a modern scholarly category applied to a diverse set of religious movements in the 1st–3rd centuries CE sharing: a demiurgic cosmology (the material world created by an inferior deity, not the highest God), pneumatic anthropology (humans have a divine spark trapped in matter), and salvation through *gnosis* (knowledge/revelation). Major 'Gnostic' systems: Valentinians (Ptolemy, Theodotus), Sethians, Basilideans, Ophites, Marcionites (disputed). Primary sources: Irenaeus AH (hostile), Nag Hammadi codices (1st-hand), Hippolytus *Philosophumena* (hostile). The category 'Gnosticism' is contested: M.A. Williams (*Rethinking Gnosticism*, 1996) and others argue it is too broad to be analytically useful. In this dataset, individual groups are modeled separately (valentinians, marcionites, etc.) rather than under a single 'gnostic' group.

The Coptic *Gospel of Thomas* (Nag Hammadi Codex II,2), discovered 1945, contains 114 sayings attributed to Jesus. Its relationship to the canonical Gospels is debated: some scholars argue it preserves independent early traditions; others see it as dependent on the Synoptics and/or developing Gnostic tendencies. The work shows no narrative structure, passion account, or resurrection appearances. Greek fragments (*P.Oxy.* 1, 654, 655) predate the Coptic version. The date ranges from very early (some scholars: 50–70 CE) to mid-2nd century (majority scholarly position: c. 120–140 CE). Proposition claims based on Gospel of Thomas are tagged `possible` or `probable` given the uncertainty about its date, provenance, and theological character.

[[person:gregory-the-illuminator|Gregory the Illuminator]] (c. 239–330 CE) is the apostle of Armenia and first bishop of the Armenian church. **Biography**: Born of Parthian nobility; imprisoned 13 years in a pit by King Tiridates III after refusing to sacrifice to the goddess Anahit; healed Tiridates of a mental illness (per tradition); converted him to Christianity c. 301 CE — making Armenia the first nation to adopt Christianity as a state religion. **Consecration**: Gregory was consecrated bishop by Leontius of Caesarea in Cappadocia; he established his episcopal see at Vagharshapat (later Etchmiadzin). **Primary source**: The Armenian source *Agathangelos* (c. 5th century) is the main narrative account; Rufinus HE 1.9, Socrates HE 1.20, and Sozomen HE 2.8 provide Greek witnesses. **Significance**: The Armenian Apostolic Church traces its foundation to Gregory; his dynasty (*Gregorids*) held the catholicate hereditarily for several generations. **Dataset note**: [[place:vagharshapat|Vagharshapat]] claims reference Gregory's episcopal seat; evidence is primarily the Socrates HE 1.19 passage.

[[person:gregory-thaumaturgus|Gregory Thaumaturgus]] (c. 213–270 CE) was a student of [[person:origen-of-alexandria|Origen]] at Caesarea Maritima, whose *Address to Origen* (c. 238 CE) is the most complete surviving firsthand account of Origen's school and teaching methods. After studying under Origen for five years, Gregory became bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, reportedly converting nearly all its pagan population — hence 'Thaumaturgus' (Wonder-Worker). His *Creed of Gregory* is one of the earliest extant extra-biblical trinitarian creeds. His biography (by Gregory of Nyssa, c. 380 CE) is hagiographically embellished and historically unreliable for the miraculous elements. The `teacher_of` relationship between Origen and Gregory is attested by Gregory's own words in the *Address to Origen*, making it one of the most secure teacher-student relationships in the patristic data.

The `group_present_at` predicate models the presence of a Christian community or sect in a geographic place at a given time. The evidence standards vary: (1) `attested` (certain=1): an ancient source explicitly names the group in that place. (2) `probable` (cert=0.7): strong inference from multiple contextual sources, e.g., a letter addressing a community there, or a bishop's see named for the place. (3) `possible` (cert=0.5): a single indirect reference, or later tradition. Examples: the Marcionite church at Rome is attested by Justin (*1 Apol* 26), Irenaeus (AH 1.27), and Tertullian (*Adv. Marc.*). The Valentinians at Rome are attested by Irenaeus AH 3.4. By contrast, 'docetists at Phrygia' is modeled as `probable` because Ignatius warns against docetists addressed in Asia letters, and Phrygia is in that region, but no source explicitly names a Phrygian docetist community. Certainty levels on group_present_at claims reflect these distinctions.

The authorship of the Epistle to the Hebrews is one of the most debated questions in NT scholarship. The letter is anonymous; the Pauline attribution in the KJV title ('The Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews') has no manuscript support. Ancient proposals include Barnabas (Tertullian), Apollos (Luther, Montefiore), Priscilla (Harnack), Luke, and Clement of Rome. Origen famously concluded: 'who actually wrote the epistle, only God knows' (Eusebius HE 6.25.14). The letter's Greek style is distinct from Paul's authenticated letters. No `authored_by` claim is made for Hebrews in this dataset; any authorship claim should be marked `possible` or `claimed_tradition` at best.

The Epistle to the Hebrews presents the most complex authorship problem in the NT. The letter is anonymous; Paul's name appears in no manuscript. Ancient attributions: Origen (*c.* 230 CE, in Eusebius HE 6.25.11–14): 'Who wrote the epistle, in truth God knows' — while noting the thought is Pauline but the style is better Greek than Paul. Tertullian attributed it to Barnabas. Clement of Alexandria: Luke translated Paul's Hebrew original (Eusebius HE 6.14.2). Modern scholarly options: Paul, Barnabas, Luke, Apollos (Luther's suggestion), Priscilla (Harnack), or an unknown Pauline school author. Style analysis: Hebrews has the most polished Greek in the NT, with periodic sentences and extensive use of *qal wahomer* (lesser-to-greater) argument — very different from Paul's authentic letters. In this dataset, Pauline authorship claims carry `possible` certainty; Alexandrian/Pauline-school authorship carries `probable`.

Hegesippus (c. 110–180 CE) was a Jewish Christian apologist whose five-volume *Memoirs* (*Hypomnemata*) are lost except in extensive quotations by Eusebius. His significance: (1) He provides the earliest episcopal succession list for Rome (Eusebius HE 4.22.3), which he compiled during a journey from Corinth to Rome; (2) He is the primary source for the tradition of James the Lord's brother and his martyrdom; (3) He used the term *ekklesia* to distinguish the true church from heretical communities. Eusebius describes Hegesippus as visiting many bishops and finding the same teaching (*didache*) everywhere — an early appeal to apostolic consensus. His Jewish-Christian perspective and proximity to the Palestinian tradition make him an important (if fragmentarily preserved) witness to 2nd-century catholicism. All claims derived from Hegesippus are mediated through Eusebius's selective quotation.

[[bible:Col.4.12-Col.4.13|Colossians 4:12-13]] explicitly attests believers in [[place:hierapolis]] through Epaphras's concern, but it does not explicitly name a distinct church there. This batch therefore records generic disciple presence rather than creating a new communion entity.

The *Apostolic Tradition* attributed to [[person:hippolytus-of-rome|Hippolytus of Rome]] (c. 215 CE) is one of the most important early Christian liturgical documents, preserving the eucharistic prayer, baptismal rite, ordination prayers, and community regulations. However, its attribution to Hippolytus is strongly contested. The current critical consensus (Bradshaw, Johnson, Phillips) questions both Hippolytine authorship and Roman provenance. The text may be a composite document from the 3rd–4th centuries, possibly from Egypt or Syria. Despite this, it remains significant evidence for early liturgical practice. Claims about the *Apostolic Tradition*'s propositions are modeled as `probable` for Hippolytine authorship and `attested` for the liturgical content itself (which is independently attested regardless of exact authorship).

The rivalry between [[person:hippolytus-of-rome|Hippolytus]] and [[person:callistus-i|Callistus I]] (bishop of Rome 217–222 CE) involved both theological and disciplinary disputes. Hippolytus accused Callistus of modalism (Sabellianism) and of laxity in admitting the lapsed and clerics who had remarried. The Philosophumena (Refutation of All Heresies) is Hippolytus's polemical account. The historicity of Hippolytus's own counter-episcopacy is debated: the Liberian Catalogue lists him as a schismatic bishop. He was ultimately reconciled to Rome and martyred with Pope Pontian under Maximinus Thrax (235 CE). Claims modeling his `rival_bishop` role are attested from Hippolytus's own polemical writings, filtered through his obvious bias against Callistus.
Novatian's De Trinitate shows strong influence from Hippolytus's Logos theology. The teacher_of claim is modeled as probable based on theological dependence and Roman church context.
Hippolytus established a rival episcopal succession against Callistus I c. 217. Modeled as probable to reflect contested status.

[[person:ignatius-of-antioch|Ignatius of Antioch]] wrote seven letters while being transported to martyrdom in Rome (c. 107–117 CE under Trajan): to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, Smyrna, and to [[person:polycarp-of-smyrna|Polycarp]]. These survive in three recensions: Short (Syriac, 3 letters), Middle (Greek, 7 letters — accepted as authentic), and Long (spurious expansions). The Middle Recension is the scholarly consensus for authenticity (Lightfoot, Zahn, against Downer and Pearson's challenges). Ignatius is the primary early source for: monarchical episcopate, the Eucharist as 'medicine of immortality,' anti-docetic polemic, and martyrdom theology. The exact year is uncertain (Trajan reign = 98–117 CE); 107–115 CE is the standard range. See also note `note-ignatius-middle-recension`.

[[person:ignatius-of-antioch|Ignatius]]'s martyrdom at Rome (c. 107–117 CE) is attested by the seven authentic letters themselves — written en route to Rome — and by Polycarp's *Epistle to the Philippians* 13 (which asks for news of Ignatius). However, no independent contemporary account of the actual execution survives. The *Martyrium Ignatii Antiocheni* is a later legendary account, probably 4th-5th century, with historically unreliable details. Eusebius (*HE* 3.36) reports Ignatius's martyrdom under Trajan (98–117 CE). The year c. 107–117 CE is therefore `probable`: we know it was during Trajan's reign, the letters confirm transport to Rome, and Rome is the implied destination (*Ign. Rom.* passim). The exact year cannot be established. Ignatius's theology of martyrdom: he actively seeks martyrdom, warns the Romans not to intercede on his behalf, describes the wild beasts as grinding him into 'pure bread for Christ' — the most developed early theology of voluntary martyrdom.

The seven letters of [[person:ignatius-of-antioch|Ignatius]] in the middle recension (Eph, Magn, Trall, Rom, Phil, Smyrn, Polyc) are widely accepted as authentic (Lightfoot, Zahn, Schoedel). The longer and shorter recensions are rejected as interpolated/abbreviated. All claims based on Ignatius's letters use the middle recension.

[[work:against-heresies|Against Heresies]] (*Adversus Haereses*) was composed in stages by [[person:irenaeus-of-lyons|Irenaeus]] c. 175–185 CE. The five-book work's internal evidence (AH 2.22.5 reference to 'those who have seen John' as still living) suggests the early books were written c. 175–180 CE; the later books likely c. 180–185 CE. It is the most comprehensive anti-heretical treatise of the 2nd century, surveying Valentinian, Marcionite, Basilidean, and other Gnostic systems. AH 3.3.1–4 contains the famous Roman episcopal succession list (Peter → Linus → Anacletus → Clement → ...) and the appeal to apostolic tradition. Book 5's eschatology and millennialism are unique among Irenaeus's preserved positions. The original Greek is largely lost; the work survives in a close Latin translation and in Armenian and Syriac fragments.

AH 2.22.4 states Christ "became an infant for infants" and sanctified every age. This is the standard patristic citation for infant baptism theology, but the text does not use the word "baptism" explicitly. The claim is modeled as attested because Origen (Comm. Romans 5.9) cites "the tradition from the apostles" for infant baptism and presupposes Irenaeus is in that stream. Certainty is attested but the inference path is one level indirect.

[[person:irenaeus-of-lyons|Irenaeus]] (*AH* 3.1.1–3.3.4) is the first author to explicitly name and argue for a four-Gospel canon: Matthew (for Hebrew Jews), Mark (Peter's preaching), Luke (Paul's Gospel), John (for the Logos). His argument for exactly four Gospels from AH 3.11.8 is famous: 'there are four principal winds, four quarters of the world, four living creatures before the throne — therefore four Gospels.' Irenaeus also accepted the Pauline epistles (including the Pastorals and Hebrews), Acts, Revelation, and 1 John as authoritative Scripture. He is thus the earliest witness to a recognizably 'canonical' NT core. His acceptance of Revelation against Gaius (who rejected it as Cerinthian) is significant for Revelation's canonical history. Claims about Irenaeus's canonical positions are modeled as `attested` based on explicit statements in *Against Heresies* and his surviving fragments.

[[person:irenaeus-of-lyons|Irenaeus]]'s *anakephalaiosis* (recapitulation) theology — first fully developed in AH 3 and 5 — holds that Christ recapitulates (*anakepha-laioō*) all humanity in himself, retracing and undoing Adam's steps. Adam disobeyed at a tree (the forbidden fruit); Christ obeys on a tree (the cross). Adam was made of virgin earth; Christ born of a virgin. Adam fell in a garden; Christ's agony begins in Gethsemane. The recapitulation motif requires the full humanity of Christ — making it both anti-Docetist and anti-Marcionite. Irenaeus's recapitulation is also the basis for his 'physical redemption' soteriology: Christ became what we are so that we might become what he is (*AH* 5.praef.). This proposition is attested in AH 3.18-22 and 5.1-21 and is modeled as `attested` in the dataset under the `work_affirms_proposition` predicate for Against Heresies.

[[person:jacob-of-nisibis|Jacob of Nisibis]] (died c. 338 CE) was the first bishop of [[place:nisibis|Nisibis]] (modern Nusaybin, Turkey/Syria border) and the spiritual father of [[person:ephrem-the-syrian|Ephrem the Syrian]]. **Historical role**: - Bishop of Nisibis from c. 308 CE; - Attended the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and opposed Arius; - Credited with founding the School of Nisibis, one of the great intellectual centers of Syriac Christianity; - Participated in the defense of Nisibis against Persian sieges. **Sources**: Ephrem's *Carmina Nisibena* (Hymns of Nisibis) are the most important primary witness to Jacob's life and work; Theodoret *HE* 1.7 also mentions him. **Nisibis**: After the Roman cession of Nisibis to Persia in 363 CE (following Julian's defeat), the Christian community and school relocated to Edessa, then later re-established. **Dataset note**: The Jacob-Ephrem teacher relationship is a central claim in this dataset's Syriac Christianity coverage; Ephrem's own hymns are the strongest evidence.

The fate of the Jerusalem church after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem (70 CE) is important for understanding early Jewish Christianity. Eusebius (*HE* 3.5.3) reports the Jerusalem Christians fled to Pella in Transjordan before the siege — the 'Pella flight' tradition. This is accepted by many scholars but questioned by others (Brandon, Weiss) as a late apologetic construction. After 70 CE, Jerusalem/Aelia Capitolina (renamed after 135 CE) had a gentile-majority Christian community under a non-Jewish bishop (Marcus, according to Eusebius HE 4.6). Jewish Christians (Ebionites, Nazarenes) survived in Transjordan, Syria, and Egypt. Claims about the Jerusalem church's presence and leadership after 70 CE carry `probable` certainty and depend heavily on Eusebius, whose reliability for this period is uncertain.

The Johannine authorship question encompasses the Gospel, three epistles, and Revelation. The traditional view: the Apostle John (son of Zebedee) wrote all five. The critical problems: (1) Dionysius of Alexandria (*c.* 260 CE, in Eusebius HE 7.25) first argued that Revelation and the Gospel/Epistles are by different authors based on Greek style. (2) The Gospel and 1 John share vocabulary and theology closely; 2–3 John identify the author as 'the Elder.' (3) Papias (*c.* 130 CE) distinguishes 'John the Apostle' from 'John the Elder,' suggesting two Johns at Ephesus. Current scholarly positions: - Gospel: probably the 'Beloved Disciple' community at Ephesus, c. 90–100 CE. - 1 John: same tradition, slightly later. - 2–3 John: 'the Elder,' probably the same author as 1 John. - Revelation: different author, probably 'John the Elder' or an unknown John. Claims about Johannine authorship carry `probable` for apostolic attribution, with the note that this attribution is traditional and contested.

The tradition that John the son of Zebedee lived and died at Ephesus is one of the most important and contested claims in early church history. Evidence for: (1) Irenaeus (*AH* 3.1.1): 'John the disciple of the Lord, who also had leaned upon His breast, did himself publish a Gospel during his residence at Ephesus in Asia'; (2) Polycarp claimed to know John (via Irenaeus *Ep. Flor.* apud Eusebius HE 5.20); (3) The seven letters to Asia in Revelation 2–3 suggest Johannine authority over the Ephesian region. Evidence against: (1) Papias (*apud* Philip of Side and Georgius Hamartolus) may record that both James and John were martyred early by Jews — predating an Ephesian ministry; (2) Mk 10:39 ('you will drink my cup') might predict early martyrdom for John too; (3) The 'Elder John' of 2–3 John and Papias could be the real Ephesian leader, distinct from the Apostle. In this dataset: John's presence in Ephesus and authorship of the Fourth Gospel carry `probable` certainty, reflecting the strong Irenaean tradition against genuine uncertainty about the Apostle vs. Elder distinction.
The term bishop applied to John at Ephesus is anachronistic. Irenaeus and Polycrates name John as the apostolic authority. Modeled as probable.

The claim that John the Apostle taught Polycarp rests on [[person:irenaeus-of-lyons]]'s own statement in AH 3.3.4 and his letter to Florinus (Eusebius HE 5.20). This is not Polycarp's own claim but Irenaeus's eyewitness testimony that he heard Polycarp describe his contact with John and others who had seen Christ. The claim is modeled as attested because Irenaeus is a first-hand witness to Polycarp's teaching.

Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 CE) wrote in Greek for Roman audiences, aiming to present Judaism favorably. His works are our primary non-NT source for 1st-century Judaea. Key passages for this dataset: (1) *Ant.* 18.63–64: *Testimonium Flavianum* — Jesus reference; partial authenticity is the scholarly majority position; (2) *Ant.* 20.200: James 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ' executed c. 62 CE — widely accepted as authentic; (3) *Ant.* 18.116–119: John the Baptist — politically motivated execution by Herod Antipas; independent of Gospel accounts; (4) *JW* 2.119–166: the three Jewish philosophical schools (Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes); (5) *JW* 6.249–266: the burning of the Temple, 70 CE. Methodological note: Josephus is an apologetic historian writing under Roman patronage — he minimizes Roman atrocities and Jewish resistance. His accounts require critical analysis against archaeological evidence and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 CE) provides the most important non-Christian Jewish witness to the period of Christian origins. Key passages in this dataset: (1) *Ant.* 18.63–64 (*Testimonium Flavianum*): mentions Jesus, 'a wise man'; the current text is partly interpolated by Christian scribes (Origen does not know the 'he was the Christ' phrase; the Arabic version of Agapius preserves a more restrained original); (2) *Ant.* 20.200: death of 'James the brother of Jesus who was called Christ'; widely accepted as authentic; (3) *Ant.* 18.116–119: John the Baptist's execution by Herod Antipas for political reasons — independent of Gospel accounts; (4) *JW* 2.119ff: the three Jewish 'philosophies' (Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes), providing context for the Jewish sectarian matrix. Josephus's testimony is rated `attested` for the Jamesian and Baptist passages and `probable` for the Testimonium's historical core (bracketing interpolations).

The *Book of Jubilees* (c. 160–140 BCE, Hebrew, translated into Greek and Ethiopic; partially preserved in DSS fragments) is a retelling of Genesis–Exodus 14 structured around a 49-year 'jubilee' calendar. Canonical status: Scripture in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church; found at Qumran in 15 copies (showing its importance to the sect). Theological themes: (1) Solar calendar of 364 days (364 = 4×91; a perfect calendar with no intercalation needed); this differs from the lunar calendar used in Jerusalem and is a polemical feature; (2) Strict separation of Israel from Gentiles; (3) Detailed angelology (angels dictate the book to Moses); (4) Dating all biblical events to jubilee periods. Connection to early Christianity: the solar calendar of Jubilees may explain how Jesus could celebrate Passover on Tuesday evening while the Jerusalem authorities observed it two days later — a possible resolution of the Synoptic/Johannine chronological tension. In this dataset, Jubilees is used as contextual background for Second Temple Judaism's calendar and legal disputes.

[[person:julius-africanus|Julius Africanus]] (c. 160–c. 240 CE) was a Christian chronographer and polymath, active in both Emmaus-Nicopolis and Rome. **Works**: - *Chronographiae* (5 volumes): a world chronicle synchronizing biblical and pagan history; calculated the birth of Christ in the 5500th year since creation; influential on Eusebius's *Chronicle*; - *Kestoi* (24 books): a miscellany covering military science, medicine, magic, and natural history — dedicated to Emperor Alexander Severus; - Letters to Origen (on the Susanna narrative) and to Aristides (on the genealogies of Christ). **Career**: At the request of Emperor Alexander Severus, built a library at the Pantheon in Rome; also associated with Emmaus-Nicopolis, where he may have been a city official. Eusebius *HE* 6.31 is the primary source. **Historical significance**: His chronological system shaped patristic and Byzantine historiography; his 5500 AM date for the Incarnation differs from Eusebius's 5200 AM. **Dataset note**: Claims cover his activity in both Emmaus and Rome, attested by Eusebius HE 6.31.

[[person:justin-martyr|Justin Martyr]]'s apologetic corpus includes: (1) *First Apology* (c. 155 CE) — addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius, defending Christians against accusations and describing early Christian worship in detail; (2) *Second Apology* (c. 157 CE, or a continuation/appendix of the First) — addressed to the Roman Senate, shorter and more pointed; (3) *Dialogue with Trypho* (c. 155–160 CE) — the longest early Christian apologetic to Judaism, demonstrating that Christ fulfills Hebrew scripture. The First Apology (ch. 65–67) contains the earliest detailed description of Sunday Christian worship (reading, homily, prayers, Eucharist, collection), making it indispensable for early liturgical history. Justin's Logos theology (drawn from Middle Platonism) is the earliest sustained philosophical christology in extant sources.

[[person:justin-martyr|Justin Martyr]]'s death is attested by the *Acta Iustini* (Acts of Justin), which preserve the trial record before Prefect Rusticus in Rome c. 163–167 CE. Justin refused to sacrifice and was beheaded along with six companions. Eusebius HE 4.11–16 places his death under Marcus Aurelius. The year 165 CE is the traditional date based on the prefecture of Q. Junius Rusticus (163–168 CE). The martyrdom at Rome is confirmed by the *Acta* and by Tatian's statement that he witnessed Justin's death (Oration 19). The claim certainty `probable` reflects the 163–168 CE range of the prefectural dates.
Justin records his encounter with Trypho in Ephesus in the Dialogue prologue. His pre-Roman period likely included time in Ephesus.

[[person:justin-martyr|Justin Martyr]]'s Logos theology (*1 Apol.* 5, 21, 32–33; *2 Apol.* 6, 8, 10, 13; *Dial.* 61, 128) draws on Middle Platonism: the Logos is the first-begotten of God (*prōtotokos*), the divine Reason immanent in creation and now fully incarnate in Jesus. Crucially, Justin argues that pagan philosophers who lived 'according to the Logos' (e.g., Socrates, Heraclitus) were 'Christians before Christ' — a position that makes Greek philosophy a *praeparatio evangelica*. Justin's subordinationist tendency (the Logos is numerically distinct from the Father, generated for creation) influenced later Western theology but is distinct from Nicene co-equality. The claim `work_affirms_proposition logos-pre-existent` for Justin's works is attested with high confidence across all three major texts.

The *Letter to Diognetus* is one of the most elegant Christian apologetic texts, notable for its description of Christians as a 'third race' distinct from Jews and pagans. Date and authorship are entirely unknown; traditionally grouped with the Apostolic Fathers though its style and theology suggest a 2nd–3rd century date. The famous passage (Ep. Diog. 5–6): Christians 'live in their own countries but as aliens; they share in everything as citizens and endure everything as foreigners. Every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland is foreign... They are in the world what the soul is in the body.' Chapters 11–12 are now widely recognized as a separate document (possibly a homily by Hippolytus or another author) appended to the original letter. The only manuscript (Codex Argentoratensis) was destroyed in the Strasbourg fire of 1870 — all modern texts derive from 16th-century copies. In this dataset, *Letter to Diognetus* is used to support claims about early Christian self-understanding as a distinct religious community.

Sunday as the primary Christian worship day is well-attested by c. 100–150 CE. Key texts: (1) Acts 20:7: 'on the first day of the week...to break bread'; (2) 1 Cor 16:2: 'on the first day of every week, set aside money'; (3) Rev 1:10: 'I was in the Spirit on the Lord's Day' (*kyriakē hēmera*); (4) *Didache* 14.1: 'On the Lord's Day gather and break bread'; (5) Ignatius *Magn.* 9.1: Christians 'no longer observe the Sabbath but live by the Lord's Day'; (6) Justin *1 Apol.* 67: 'On the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or country gather together.' The transition from Sabbath to Sunday: Christian communities may have observed both initially; the shift is polemic in Ignatius (anti-Judaism), pragmatic in Justin (weekly resurrection celebration). Pliny (*Ep.* 10.96, c. 112 CE): Christians meet 'on a fixed day' before dawn — consistent with Sunday. In this dataset, Sunday gathering claims carry `attested` certainty with high confidence where direct textual witnesses name Sunday explicitly.

The Lord's Prayer (*Pater Noster*) is attested in two forms: Mt 6:9–13 (longer, liturgical, with doxology in later MSS) and Lk 11:2–4 (shorter, simpler). Most scholars regard Luke's as earlier. The *Didache* 8.2–3 quotes Matthew's version and commands: 'Pray thus three times a day' — the first evidence for structured daily Christian prayer. Tertullian (*De Oratione*, c. 198–200 CE) wrote the first extended commentary, calling it a *breviarum totius evangelii* ('summary of the whole Gospel'). Cyprian (*De Dominica Oratione*, c. 251 CE) wrote the second major commentary, emphasizing the corporate 'Our' as ecclesiological: one cannot say 'our' while outside the church. Origen (*De Oratione*, c. 233–234 CE): distinguishes prayer forms and gives detailed allegorical exegesis of each petition. The doxology ('For yours is the kingdom...') appears in the *Didache* 8.2 but not in the earliest Gospel manuscripts — likely a liturgical addition. In this dataset, 'prayer three times daily' and 'Lord's Prayer in liturgy' are coded as `work_affirms_proposition` from the Didache.

The persecution at Lyons and Vienne in 177 CE is attested by the letter of the churches of Gaul preserved in Eusebius HE 5.1–3, one of the most detailed and moving martyrdom accounts in early Christianity. It describes the torture and deaths of Blandina, Pothinus (the aged bishop), and others. [[person:irenaeus-of-lyons|Irenaeus]] was a presbyter at Lyons at this time; he was sent to Rome as an emissary and survived the persecution. The year 177 CE is confirmed by the reference to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus as co-emperors. The year claim is therefore `attested` with high confidence.

All surviving evidence for [[person:marcion-of-sinope|Marcion]]'s teachings comes from his opponents ([[person:irenaeus-of-lyons|Irenaeus]], [[person:tertullian|Tertullian]], Epiphanius). His own writings are lost. The claims about his doctrines are attested as what his opponents *described* him as teaching; there is a methodological limitation in that we cannot verify these descriptions against Marcion's own words. Tertullian's reconstruction of Marcion's Antitheses in Adv. Marcionem is the closest we get.

[[person:marcion-of-sinope|Marcion]] of Sinope (c. 85–160 CE) produced the first known Christian scriptural canon (c. 144 CE), consisting of: (1) *Evangelion* — a version of Luke's Gospel with passages Marcion regarded as Jewish interpolations removed; (2) *Apostolikon* — 10 Pauline letters (excluding the Pastorals) also edited. Debate: Did Marcion shorten an existing Gospel of Luke, or does the current Luke expand an original Marcion-like text? Majority view (Harnack, Tertullian): Marcion abridged Luke. Minority view (Tyson, BeDuhn): Marcion preserves an earlier, shorter form. Regardless, Marcion's canon provoked the proto-orthodox response that eventually produced the NT canon as we know it. Marcion's theological motivation: Paul's antithesis of Law and Gospel implies the OT God (Creator/Judge) is different from the NT God (Father of Christ). Tertullian's *Adversus Marcionem* (5 books) is the fullest refutation and the primary source for Marcion's theology.

The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* (c. 156 CE, from the church at Smyrna) is the earliest account of a Christian martyrdom outside the NT, and the first to use the term 'martyr' (*martys*) in its developed theological sense. It establishes the martyrdom paradigm: the martyr follows Christ's passion, refuses to recant, is burned but miraculously unharmed until stabbed, and his bones are venerated as 'more precious than gold.' Date debate: the text gives the date as 23 February in the proconsulship of Statius Quadratus, which most scholars date to c. 156 CE; some argue for 167 CE. The account includes a secondary narrative of Quintus, who initially volunteered for martyrdom but apostatized — contrasted with Polycarp's model comportment. The anniversary celebration of the martyrdom at Polycarp's tomb is the first attested Christian commemoration of a martyr — the foundation of the saints' calendar tradition. Year claims for this event carry `probable` certainty given the proconsular dating ambiguity.

[[person:melito-of-sardis|Melito of Sardis]] (d. c. 180 CE) was bishop of Sardis and one of the most prolific 2nd-century Christian writers. Almost all his works are lost; only the *Peri Pascha* (*On the Passover*) survives complete (discovered in Papyrus Bodmer XIII, 1960). Key contributions: (1) First known Christian list of OT canonical books (Eusebius HE 4.26.14), which closely matches the Hebrew Bible but includes Wisdom; (2) *Peri Pascha* is the most vivid example of early Christian anti-Judaism, with its 'God has been murdered' polemic — important for the history of Christian antisemitism; (3) First explicit use of the term 'Old Testament' (*palaia diatheke*) in Christian literature; (4) He was a Quartodeciman, celebrating Easter on Nisan 14 regardless of weekday. Melito's *Peri Pascha* is also significant as the first developed liturgical homily in Christian literature, displaying elaborate rhetorical artistry.

[[work:homily-on-the-passover|Melito of Sardis's *Peri Pascha*]] (c. 160–170 CE) is the earliest complete Christian sermon, recovered in its full Syriac and Greek forms only in the 20th century. It is a typological homily on the Passover interpreted christologically, notable for its rich rhetorical style, explicit anti-Jewish rhetoric, and early high-Christology (52: 'God has been murdered'). Melito was Quartodeciman (Eusebius HE 4.26), celebrating Easter on 14 Nisan. The *Peri Pascha* is the primary source for Quartodeciman paschal theology. Some scholars see the anti-Jewish polemic as a response to a vigorous Jewish community in Sardis; the Sardis synagogue is the largest known ancient synagogue.

Monarchianism is the theological tendency to preserve the 'monarchy' (single rule) of God by stressing divine unity over trinitarian distinction. Two types: (1) *Dynamic/Adoptionist*: Jesus was a human being who was 'adopted' into divine sonship at baptism — represented by Theodotus the Cobbler (Rome, c. 190 CE), Artemon, and Paul of Samosata. (2) *Modalist/Patripassianist*: Father, Son, and Spirit are three modes of one divine Person — represented by Noetus of Smyrna, Praxeas (c. 200 CE, attacked by Tertullian's *Adv. Praxean*), and Sabellius (Rome, c. 215 CE). Hippolytus accused his own bishop Callistus I of Sabellianism. Modalism was widespread at Rome in the early 3rd century. The labels 'Sabellian,' 'Patripassian,' and 'modalist' are often used interchangeably in secondary literature; they refer to the same basic position with slight variations.

The Montanist movement (New Prophecy) arose in Phrygia c. 155–172 CE under [[person:montanus|Montanus]], [[person:priscilla|Priscilla]], and Maximilla, who claimed to be vehicles of the Paraclete's new revelations. The movement emphasized the imminent parousia, strict ascetic practice, and the authority of ecstatic prophecy over episcopal hierarchy. The date of origin is uncertain (Eusebius gives varying accounts). The movement spread to Rome and Carthage (Tertullian). Montanism was condemned by Asian bishops (anonymous anti-Montanist writings cited by Eusebius HE 5.16–17) and later by synods. The theological dispute centered on whether the Paraclete could add new binding revelation after the apostolic age. The Montanist schism is classified as a disciplinary/prophetic dispute rather than a christological or trinitarian heresy.
The Montanist movement originated in Phrygia as a prophetic revival within the Asian churches. Modeled against the Ephesian church as metropolitan see of Asia.

The Muratorian Fragment (or Canon) is the earliest surviving list of NT books recognized as authoritative in a particular Christian community. Discovered by Ludovico Muratori (1740) in an 8th-century manuscript, it is written in poor Latin and probably translated from Greek. Traditional dating: c. 170–200 CE, Rome (based on its reference to Pius I as recent: 'very recently in our times'). Alternative dating: some scholars (Sundberg, Hahneman) argue for a 4th-century Eastern origin, but the traditional early Roman date remains the majority view. Contents: accepts 4 Gospels, Acts, 13 Paulines (not Hebrews), Jude, 1–2 John, Wisdom of Solomon, Revelation of John, Apocalypse of Peter (with reservation). Rejects: Marcionite epistles, Shepherd of Hermas (too recent for public use). The Fragment's value: it shows a recognizable NT core taking shape in the West by the late 2nd century, with contested periphery books.

The Neronian persecution of 64 CE is attested by Tacitus (*Annals* 15.44), who describes Nero blaming Christians for the great fire of Rome. Tacitus calls them 'hated for their abominations' (*per flagitia invisos*) and describes their execution. This is the earliest pagan witness to a Roman persecution of Christians. The connection to Peter's and Paul's martyrdoms is traditional (Eusebius, 1 Clement 5) but the exact year of their deaths is not directly stated by Tacitus. The `probable` certainty on the Peter/Paul martyrdom year reflects this: 64–68 CE is the probable range, with 64 CE traditional for the Neronian fire connection.

The original Nicene Creed of 325 CE (distinct from the 381 Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed used in liturgy today) reads in key part: *'We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father as only-begotten, that is, from the essence (οὐσίας) of the Father, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten not made, of one substance (ὁμοούσιον) with the Father...'* followed by anathemas against anyone who says: *'there was when he was not,'* or *'he did not exist before he was born,'* or *'he came into being from nothing,'* or *'he is of a different substance (ὑποστάσεως) or essence (οὐσίας) from the Father.'* **Homoousios controversy**: The term *homoousios* was not biblical and had been condemned at the Synod of Antioch (268 CE) in the Paul of Samosata controversy — a fact the Arians exploited. Athanasius spent decades defending its legitimacy in works like *De Decretis Nicaenae Synodi*. **Dataset note**: The Nicene creed text is attested in multiple sources including Eusebius's letter to his church (*apud* Theodoret *HE* 1.12) and Athanasius's writings.

[[bible:Rev.2.6|Revelation 2:6]] and [[bible:Rev.2.15|Revelation 2:15]] name the Nicolaitans through their works or teaching in [[place:ephesus]] and [[place:pergamum]]. The resulting presence claims are therefore modeled as probable group presence rather than direct census-style attestations.

[[work:de-trinitate-novatian|Novatian's *De Trinitate*]] (c. 240–250 CE) is the earliest surviving comprehensive Latin trinitarian treatise, written before Novatian's schism with Cornelius over the lapsed. It defends: the full divinity of Christ against adoptionism, the distinction of Father and Son against modalism (Sabellian monarchianism), and the monarchia (one divine rule) against apparent ditheism. The work is orthodox by Nicene standards; Novatian's later schism was disciplinary, not doctrinal. The *De Trinitate* was long misattributed to Tertullian (as the 'Adversus Praxean II') before Weyer's 1962 critical edition confirmed Novatian's authorship. Claims about Novatian's trinitarian theology derive primarily from this work and are `attested` with high confidence.

[[person:novatian|Novatian]] established a rival bishopric at Rome c. 251 CE, opposing [[person:cornelius-pope|Cornelius]] over the question of readmitting the lapsed (those who had apostatized in the Decian persecution). Novatian held that the church had no power to restore apostates even on their deathbed — a rigorist position condemned by Cyprian and the African councils. The Novatianist schism persisted until the 5th century. His `De Trinitate` is the earliest major Latin trinitarian treatise and is orthodox; his schism was disciplinary, not doctrinal.

Novatian (c. 200–258 CE) was a Roman presbyter and the first major schismatic in the West. After Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome (251 CE), Novatian had himself consecrated as a rival bishop by three provincial bishops — establishing the first known anti-pope. Cause: Novatian's rigorism — the lapsed (*lapsi*) who apostasized during the Decian persecution (249–250 CE) could never be readmitted to communion. Cyprian's middle path: the lapsed could be readmitted after appropriate penance — a prolonged period determined by their offense (offering sacrifice = longest; obtaining libellus = shorter). Novatian's theology: his *De Trinitate* (c. 250 CE) is the first extant Latin theological treatise on the Trinity and is theologically orthodox (*homoousios* equivalent) — his schism was disciplinary, not doctrinal. The Novatianist church survived into the 5th century in some areas. Significance: the debate established the Catholic principle that the unity and catholicity of the church outweigh disciplinary rigorism — a principle further developed by Augustine against the Donatists.

The NT Apocrypha includes texts that parallel NT genres (gospels, acts, epistles, apocalypses) but were not included in the 27-book canon. Major texts in this dataset's scope (0–400 CE): - *Gospel of Thomas* (NH II.2, c. 50–150 CE): 114 sayings of Jesus, possibly containing authentic independent traditions alongside gnostic redaction. - *Gospel of Peter* (fragment, c. 100–150 CE): passion and resurrection narrative. - *Protoevangelium of James* (c. 150 CE): infancy gospel; source of Mary traditions. - *Acts of Paul* (c. 160–190 CE): includes 3 Corinthians and Acts of Paul and Thecla. - *Acts of Thomas* (c. 200–225 CE): Thomas's Indian mission. - *Acts of Peter* (c. 180–190 CE): Peter's ministry and martyrdom in Rome. - *Apocalypse of Peter* (c. 100–135 CE): vivid afterlife descriptions; accepted in Muratorian Fragment with reservation. In this dataset, NT apocryphal works are used as evidence where they attest to the presence of theological traditions or historical memories, with appropriate certainty ratings reflecting their genre and distance from events.

NT canon formation was gradual, with key milestones: c. 50–100 CE: Paul's letters circulated among churches; Gospels composed. c. 100–150 CE: Gospel collections emerging; 2 Peter knows Pauline letter collection (3:15–16); Marcion's truncated canon provokes Catholic response. c. 140–180 CE: Marcion excludes OT and non-Pauline letters; Justin (*1 Apol.* 67) reads 'memoirs of the apostles' (Gospels) in worship. c. 170–200 CE: Irenaeus (AH 3.11.8) argues for four and only four Gospels; Muratorian Fragment (c. 180–200 CE) lists canonical books for Rome. c. 200–300 CE: Origen surveys canon (*Comm. Matt.* apud Eusebius HE 6.25), distinguishing *homologoumena* (agreed) from *antilegomena* (disputed). 367 CE: Athanasius's Festal Letter 39 lists all 27 NT books as canonical. 393/397 CE: Councils of Hippo and Carthage ratify the 27-book NT. Key contested books: Hebrews (West), Revelation (East), James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude. Key excluded books that circulated widely: Shepherd of Hermas, Didache, Barnabas, Apocalypse of Peter, 1 Clement.

The `addressed_to_place` predicate for NT epistles reflects explicit address lines in the letter prescript (e.g., 'to all in Rome' — Rom 1:7; 'to the Corinthians' — 1 Cor 1:2). These are direct textual attestations of intended audience, not inferences. The `attested` certainty for addressed_to_place claims on genuine Paulines is therefore appropriate. For disputed or pseudonymous letters, the address still attests the intended audience (even if not Paul's actual audience), so `attested` remains correct for the address claim while authorship claims may be `probable` or `possible`. 1 Peter's unusual multiple-province address (Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia — 1 Pet 1:1) is modeled as five separate `addressed_to_place` claims, each `attested` as explicit in the letter regardless of authorship questions. Circular letters (like Ephesians, which lacks 'in Ephesus' in some MSS) are modeled as `probable` for the place attribution.

[[person:origen-of-alexandria|Origen]]'s allegorical method (*De Principiis* 4.1–3) operates on three senses of scripture: literal/somatic, moral/psychic, and spiritual/pneumatic. He argues that some passages have no literal sense and force the reader to seek the spiritual meaning. This method, inherited from Philo of Alexandria and further developed by Origen, became the dominant exegetical approach in the Alexandrian and later Eastern traditions. Origen's allegorical readings were controversial: Methodius of Olympus and Epiphanius attacked his spiritualized eschatology (bodily resurrection questioned). The First Origenist Controversy (c. 394–403 CE) and Second Origenist Controversy (c. 543 CE, leading to his condemnation at Constantinople II) were focused on: pre-existence of souls, universal restoration (apokatastasis), and the spiritual body. These condemnations are posthumous and do not affect the attestation of his *De Principiis* propositions during his lifetime.

Origen's allegorical method (*theoria*) is his most influential and controversial contribution. Grounded in his *De Principiis* (4.1–3), he proposes three senses of Scripture: literal/bodily, moral/psychic, spiritual/pneumatic (after 1 Cor 2:14–15). The method allowed Origen to: (1) Resolve apparent Biblical contradictions by treating them as intentional flags for deeper meaning; (2) Incorporate Platonic and Stoic philosophy into Christian interpretation; (3) Defend the OT's theological value against Marcionite criticism. Controversy: at the Council of Constantinople (553 CE), fifteen anathemas against 'Origenism' were issued, targeting: pre-existence of souls, universal restoration (*apokatastasis*), and the spiritual body in resurrection. The paradox: Origen's method dominated Christian biblical interpretation for centuries (through the Alexandrian school, Ambrose, Jerome initially) while his specific theological conclusions were condemned. In this dataset, Origen's theological claims derived from his writings use `explicit` mode and `attested` certainty for what the text says he taught; `probable` for what his method implied.

[[work:commentary-on-john-origen|Origen's *Commentary on John*]] is the earliest surviving comprehensive biblical commentary in Christian history. Begun at Alexandria (books 1–5 referenced by Eusebius as written before Origen's move), continued at Caesarea. 9 of the original 32 books survive fully; fragments of others are preserved. Book 1's prologue contains Origen's famous explanation of the fourfold sense of Scripture applied to the Johannine prologue. Books 2 and 6 preserve his detailed treatment of Jn 1:1–7, providing the earliest extended Logos Christology exegesis. The *Commentary on John* is the primary source for Origen's high Christology and his subordinationist tendency (the Logos is 'second God', *deuteros theos*). Proposition claims about Origen's Logos theology derive primarily from this work.

[[person:origen-of-alexandria|Origen]] was expelled from Alexandria by Bishop Demetrius c. 231 CE following his unauthorized ordination by Palestinian bishops (Eusebius HE 6.8, 6.23). He settled at Caesarea Maritima where he continued his prolific writing and teaching until his death c. 253/254 CE. The `active_in=caesarea` claims post-231 are therefore attested; the `active_in=alexandria` claims are bounded to his pre-231 period. His ordination controversy is not a heresy trial — Origen remained orthodox.

Origen's *Hexapla* (c. 230–240 CE, compiled at Caesarea Maritima) was an unprecedented six-column critical edition of the Old Testament in Hebrew and Greek: (1) Hebrew text, (2) Hebrew transliterated in Greek letters, (3) Aquila's translation, (4) Symmachus's translation, (5) Origen's revised Septuagint with critical marks (*obeli* and *asterisci*), (6) Theodotion's translation. For some books a seventh and eighth column existed (*Octapla*). The Hexapla itself (estimated at 6,000 pages) was too large to copy; only Origen's revised LXX column (column 5) was copied and circulated, becoming the basis for subsequent LXX manuscripts. The Hexapla demonstrates Origen's commitment to textual scholarship — his use of the Hebrew text against Marcionite claims and his awareness of LXX variants make it the most sophisticated critical work in early Christian biblical scholarship.

Origen's homilies represent a significant portion of his surviving output, mostly preserved in Latin translations by Rufinus of Aquileia and Jerome. Key collections: Homilies on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, Psalms, Song of Songs, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Luke. The Greek originals survive for: 20 Homilies on Jeremiah (complete), a few on Psalms. Origen's homilies were preached at Caesarea after his ordination as presbyter c. 230 CE — the first dated instance of a scholar being employed as a regular preacher. They represent popular instruction rather than scholarly commentary, using allegorical interpretation for congregational edification. Jerome's translations sometimes soften or correct what he considered theologically problematic; Rufinus's are generally more faithful. Proposition claims derived from Origen's homilies carry `attested` certainty with medium confidence (reflecting the Latin translation layer), except where the Greek original survives.

[[work:on-prayer-origen|Origen's *On Prayer*]] (c. 233–234 CE) is addressed to his patron Ambrose and Tatiana. It is the most comprehensive early Christian treatise on prayer: covering the theology of prayer, Lord's Prayer exegesis, posture in prayer (standing, facing east), and types of prayer. Notably, Origen argues that prayer should be directed to the Father *through* the Son — not to Christ directly — which became controversial. The work is a primary source for: liturgical posture, the Lord's Prayer tradition, and early pneumatology. Its authorship by Origen is uncontested; its date is established by Eusebius HE 6.18 and internal references to Ambrose.

One of the most controversial teachings attributed to [[person:origen-of-alexandria|Origen]] is the pre-existence of souls (*De Principiis* 1.5–8; 2.8–9). Origen taught that rational beings (*logikoi*) were created as equal minds (*noes*) in the beginning; their varying degrees of cooling/falling away determined their embodiment as angels, humans, or demons. The material world is thus a remedial school for fallen souls. This was condemned as heretical at the Second Council of Constantinople (553 CE), 15 anathemas against 'Origenism.' However, it is disputed how much of condemned 'Origenism' reflects Origen himself vs. Evagrius Ponticus (d. 399 CE) who systemized Origen's ideas more radically. The pre-existence teaching survives in Rufinus's Latin translation of *De Principiis*, which may soften the more problematic formulations. Claims derived from *De Principiis* about pre-existence are modeled as `attested` for the proposition itself, with the authorial note flagging the transmission problem.

Origen's threefold (or fourfold) sense of Scripture is foundational for medieval Christian hermeneutics: (1) *Somatic/literal* — the plain historical meaning; (2) *Psychic/moral* — the ethical application for the soul; (3) *Pneumatic/spiritual/allegorical* — the deeper theological or eschatological meaning, accessible to the mature Christian. Origen derived this from the Stoic threefold analysis of texts and applied it systematically in *De Principiis* 4.1–3 and throughout his commentaries. He insisted the literal sense is always true but sometimes deficient — when the literal reading is absurd or immoral, this signals that the spiritual sense is the intended meaning. The claim `work_affirms_proposition allegorical-interpretation` is `attested` for *De Principiis*, Origen's *Commentary on John*, and his *Homilies* across multiple books of Scripture. Origen's method was later criticized by Epiphanius and Jerome, and post-553 CE condemnation of 'Origenism' partly targeted his allegorical excesses.

Papias of Hierapolis (c. 60–130 CE) wrote a five-volume *Exposition of the Dominical Oracles* — entirely lost except for fragments preserved in Eusebius (*HE* 3.39) and Irenaeus (*AH* 5.33.3–4). Key fragments: (1) HE 3.39.3–4: Papias preferred oral tradition from 'the elders' over written documents — 'a living and abiding voice is worth more than any book'; (2) HE 3.39.15: 'Matthew composed the oracles (*logia*) in the Hebrew language'; 'Mark, who had been Peter's interpreter, wrote down accurately everything he remembered of what was said and done by the Lord' — the foundational texts for Gospel authorship tradition; (3) HE 3.39.11: Papias knew Aristion and the Elder John 'personally'; (4) Millennial kingdom: Papias describes a lavish earthly millennium — derided by Eusebius as 'very limited in understanding.' Papias is the crucial link between the apostolic generation and the mid-2nd century: his testimony about Gospel authorship is the earliest external evidence but is itself secondhand. In this dataset: Papias's testimony is rated `probable` — reliable tradition but not firsthand apostolic data.

Papias (Frag 1 apud Eusebius HE 3.39.4) says he inquired about what "the elders" said, including John and Matthew. Eusebius himself debated whether this John is the Apostle or "the Elder John." Irenaeus takes it as the Apostle. The claim teacher_of is modeled as probable (not attested) to reflect this ambiguity in Eusebius's own commentary.

The three Pastoral Epistles (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus) share distinctive vocabulary (175 hapax legomena not found in the seven authentic Paulines), theological concerns (church order, sound doctrine against heresy, bishop/elder qualifications), and a more settled institutional setting than Paul's authentic letters. Scholarly consensus: pseudonymous, written c. 80–100 CE by a Pauline disciple. Minority view: authentic Paulines from a later period of Paul's ministry, possibly after a hypothetical release from the Acts 28 imprisonment. The Pastorals are the primary NT source for the episcopate/presbyterate/diaconate distinction. They are the first NT works to use the term *episkopos* in a way that resembles the later monarchical bishop. Claims about Pastoral Epistles propositions are modeled as `probable` for Pauline authorship; the propositional content of the letters is modeled as attested regardless of authorship since the text is not in dispute, only who wrote it.

Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch c. 260–268 CE, was condemned for heresy at the Synod of Antioch (268 CE). He is the primary exponent of 'homoousios' in a heretical sense before Nicaea — he used the term to describe the Father and Son as 'of the same substance' in a modalist way. Ironically, Nicaea (325 CE) later redeployed 'homoousios' in an orthodox sense against Arius. His Christology was adoptionist: Jesus was a man uniquely indwelt by the divine Logos/Wisdom but not pre-existent. He reportedly introduced choral singing of hymns to himself in the liturgy. Primary sources: the synodal letter (preserved in Eusebius HE 7.27–30, 7.32). Paul's own writings are lost. Claims about his theology are mediated through hostile conciliar sources and should be marked accordingly.

The Pauline corpus includes seven letters universally accepted as authentic (Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon) and six whose authorship is disputed by modern scholarship. Deutero-Pauline: Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians (probably pseudonymous). Pastoral Epistles (1–2 Timothy, Titus): almost certainly pseudonymous by scholarly consensus, written 80–100 CE in Paul's name. All `authored_by=paul` claims for these disputed letters are modeled as `probable` or `claimed_tradition` in this dataset to reflect the scholarly consensus. The ancient church accepted all thirteen as Pauline without question.

The 'household codes' (*Haustafel*) in the Pauline corpus (Eph 5:22–6:9; Col 3:18–4:1; 1 Pet 2:18–3:7; Titus 2:1–10; 1 Tim 2:8–15, 6:1–2) address the three pairs: wife/husband, children/father, slave/master. Their origin is debated: drawn from Hellenistic-Jewish ethics (Philo, Josephus), Stoic philosophy, or an early Christian tradition (Balch, Elliott). Theological significance: the codes represent a 'patriarchalization' of the early church — accommodating the Christian community to the surrounding Greco-Roman social structure, possibly in response to external criticism. This contrasts with: Gal 3:28 ('neither slave nor free, neither male nor female'), the apparent leadership of women in Pauline communities (Rom 16), and the egalitarian ethos of some house churches. The tension between Gal 3:28 and the household codes is a key hermeneutical debate in NT scholarship. In this dataset, claims about early Christian social ethics derive primarily from the letter texts themselves and are not assigned to 'Pauline school' vs 'authentic Paul' categories.

Roman persecution of Christians was episodic, local, and legally ambiguous until the 3rd century. Key phases: (1) Neronian (64 CE): local, after the Roman fire; extra-judicial mob violence. (2) Domitianic (c. 81–96 CE): likely localized; debated how systematic. (3) Trajanic (c. 112 CE): Pliny's letter shows prosecution only when denounced, no active search; recantation accepted. (4) Hadrianic/Antonine rescripts: required proper accusation and proof. (5) Decian (249–251 CE): first empire-wide edict requiring universal sacrifice. (6) Valerianic (257–260 CE): targeted clergy and property. (7) Diocletianic/Great Persecution (303–313 CE): most severe, four edicts. The dataset models each persecution as a distinct event with `event_has_year` and participant claims for known martyrs and confessors. Years marked `attested` draw on contemporary sources; years marked `probable` reflect uncertainty in martyrology dating.

Simon Peter (Aramaic: *Kêphâ* = Rock; Greek: *Petros*) is the most prominent figure in the Synoptic Gospels and Acts. Key data points: (1) Galilean fisherman, brother of Andrew (Mk 1:16; Mt 4:18); (2) Called first among the Twelve; named 'Cephas/Peter' by Jesus (Mk 3:16; Jn 1:42); (3) Leader of the Jerusalem church after the resurrection (Gal 1:18; Acts 1–5); (4) Key figure at the Jerusalem Council c. 48 CE (Gal 2:7–8); (5) Rebuked by Paul at Antioch over table fellowship (Gal 2:11–14); (6) Presence in Rome: attested by 1 Clem 5:4, Ignatius *Rom* 4:3 ('I do not command you as Peter and Paul did'); implied by 1 Pet 5:13 ('Babylon'); (7) Martyrdom at Rome under Nero: probable (c. 64–68 CE). The Vatican tradition of Peter's burial at St Peter's Basilica: archaeological excavations 1940–1949 found a 2nd-century shrine (*tropaion*) above remains identified as possibly Petrine; most Catholic archaeologists accept this identification; Protestant scholars remain cautious. In this dataset, claims about Peter in Rome and his martyrdom carry `probable` certainty based on early literary attestation.
Patristic tradition names Peter as first bishop of Antioch. Formal episcopal terminology is anachronistic for Peter.
Irenaeus AH 3.3.1-3 names Peter as co-founder of the Roman church. Modeled as probable because monarchical episcopacy postdates Peter.

[[bible:Phlm.1.1-Phlm.1.2|Philemon 1:1-2]] names the household-church circle, and [[bible:Col.4.17|Colossians 4:17]] places [[person:archippus]] inside the Colossian closing frame. The resulting Colossae links for [[work:epistle-to-philemon]], [[person:philemon]], [[person:apphia]], and [[person:archippus]] are therefore modeled as probable contextual connections rather than direct place formulas.

Paul's letter to Philemon (c. 54–62 CE) is the most personal and legally specific of his letters, concerning the slave Onesimus. Paul's argument: (1) Onesimus has become a Christian under Paul ('my child'); (2) Paul sends him back to Philemon with a formal recommendation letter; (3) Paul hints strongly (but does not command) that Philemon manumit Onesimus ('that you might have him back forever, no longer as a slave, but better than a slave — as a dear brother,' v.15–16). The letter does not condemn slavery as an institution — Paul works within existing social structures. This has been both cited in defense of slavery (antebellum US) and critiqued as insufficient by abolitionists. Interpretation debate: Is Paul requesting manumission? Most scholars say yes (Nordling, Callahan), though some argue Paul is only asking for Onesimus's return as a co-worker (Callahan). The letter's preservation in the canon may itself testify to Philemon acting on Paul's request — i.e., Onesimus was freed and became a church leader.

The `place_presence_status` predicate records when a place first appears in Christian historical sources — not when it was settled or founded. A `place_presence_status=attested_late` value signals that the place first appears in Christian contexts only in later sources (4th century+), even if the place itself is ancient. This matters for places like: Pontus (attested in 1 Peter's address, c. 60–100 CE, but Christian community details only in Pliny's letter c. 112 CE), Cappadocia (1 Peter address), Bithynia (Pliny's letter to Trajan, c. 112 CE, the earliest explicit reference to Christians in that province), Dalmatia (2 Tim 4:10 mentions it, but only as a travel destination, not a community). The year_start on place_presence_status claims represents the earliest textual attestation date in our sources, with certainty levels reflecting source reliability.

Pliny the Younger's letter to Emperor Trajan (*Ep.* 10.96, c. 112 CE) is the earliest surviving pagan description of Christian worship practice and the first external evidence of Christian hymnody. Key data: (1) Christians sing hymns 'to Christ as to a god' (*carmen Christo quasi deo*) antiphonally; (2) They take an oath not to commit theft, robbery, or adultery; (3) Deaconesses (*ministrae*) are mentioned; (4) They meet on a fixed day (Sunday) before dawn and again to eat; (5) The practice had spread through 'city, villages, and rural areas' of Bithynia. Pliny's procedure: denounced Christians are examined; those who persist are executed not for crimes but for their name's obstinacy. Roman citizens are sent to Rome. Trajan's rescript (10.97): do not seek them out; anonymous accusations unacceptable; give opportunity to recant. This evidence is foundational for: early Christian worship reconstruction, the legal status of Christianity, and regional spread in Asia Minor c. 112 CE.

The relationship between [[person:ignatius-of-antioch|Ignatius of Antioch]] and [[person:polycarp-of-smyrna|Polycarp of Smyrna]] is one of the most significant in early Christianity. Primary evidence: Ignatius wrote a personal letter to Polycarp (one of his seven authentic letters) while en route to martyrdom in Rome, addressing him as an established bishop and giving pastoral advice. Polycarp's *Epistle to the Philippians* (Pol. Phil. 13) refers to Ignatius's letters and asks for information about Ignatius. The teacher-student claim (`clm-ignatius-teacher-of-polycarp`) draws on the testimony that Polycarp was a disciple of John (disputed — see `note-papias-john-elder`) and that Ignatius addressed him as a fellow bishop, not as a student per se. The `teacher_of` predicate here is used in the broader sense of theological influence rather than a formal school relationship. Certainty is `probable` because no source explicitly calls Polycarp Ignatius's student.

The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* is the earliest surviving Christian martyrdom account outside the New Testament, written as a letter from the church of Smyrna to the church of Philomelium shortly after the event. The date is disputed: the traditional 155/156 CE (based on the proconsulship of Statius Quadratus) is challenged by those who prefer 167/168 CE or even 177 CE. The martyrdom account reports Polycarp's age as 86 years in the faith, which would place his conversion c. 69–81 CE — consistent with contact with the apostolic generation. The claim certainty is `probable` for the year due to this prosopographical uncertainty.

[[work:epistle-of-polycarp-to-philippians|Polycarp's Epistle to the Philippians]] is a composite document: scholars (Harrison, 1936) have argued chapters 13–14 were written c. 110 CE (contemporaneous with Ignatius, while Polycarp was still alive) and chapters 1–12 were written c. 135–137 CE (after the death of Valens the presbyter mentioned in ch. 11). Most scholars now accept the letter as a unity written c. 110–120 CE. The letter is the primary source for: Polycarp's teaching on righteousness, his anti-docetic polemic ('every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is an antichrist' — *Phil* 7.1, quoting 1 John 4:2), and his catalog of virtues for church officers. It quotes or alludes to Matthew, Philippians, Ephesians, 1–2 Thessalonians, 1–2 Timothy, 1 Peter, 1 John, and 1 Clement — making it important evidence for early 2nd-century NT usage.
Polycarp visited Rome under Anicetus c. 155 to discuss Easter date. The formal Quartodeciman controversy is dated c. 190-195 under Victor, but the Polycarp-Anicetus precedent is crucial context.

The evolution from collegial presbyters to monarchical bishops is one of the most debated developments in early church history. NT evidence: Phil 1:1 (bishops and deacons, no monarchical bishop); Acts 20:17/28 (elders = bishops, used interchangeably); 1 Tim 3:1–7 (single bishop, plural deacons); Titus 1:5–7 (elders = bishops). Early 2nd century: [[person:ignatius-of-antioch|Ignatius]] (c. 107–117 CE) is the first unambiguous witness to a single monarchical bishop presiding over presbyters and deacons — but this structure he describes as the norm for Asia Minor and Syria, not necessarily universal. Rome: 1 Clement (c. 96 CE) shows no monarchical bishop — it writes from 'the church' to Corinth, naming no individual bishop. By c. 150–180 CE, monarchical episcopate is attested in Rome (Hegesippus, Irenaeus) and is rapidly becoming universal. The `bishop_of` predicate in this dataset uses `probable` certainty for figures before c. 110 CE to reflect the ongoing presbyteral-episcopal ambiguity.

[[person:priscilla|Priscilla]] (also Prisca) and [[person:aquila|Aquila]] are among the most significant figures in Pauline Christianity. They appear in six NT texts: Acts 18:2, 18, 26; Rom 16:3; 1 Cor 16:19; 2 Tim 4:19. Key features: (1) Consistently named together, usually with Priscilla first (unusual for a woman); (2) Jewish Christian tentmakers from Pontus expelled from Rome under Claudius (c. 49 CE, Acts 18:2); (3) They hosted a church in their home at Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome; (4) They corrected Apollos's theology at Ephesus (Acts 18:26); (5) Paul calls them 'my co-workers in Christ Jesus' who 'risked their necks' for him (Rom 16:3–4). The theory that Priscilla authored Hebrews (Harnack, 1900) is based on: the anonymous authorship, the 'we' of Heb 13:18, the woman-led house church context, and the Pauline connections. It remains a minority scholarly view. The `active_in` and `coworker_of` claims for Priscilla/Aquila carry `attested` certainty for Corinth and Ephesus, `probable` for Rome.

[[bible:1Cor.16.19|1 Corinthians 16:19]] names the house church of [[person:aquila]] and [[person:priscilla]], but the city is inferred from the letter's Asia/Ephesus setting rather than repeated explicitly in the verse. Their [[group:ephesian-church]] affiliations are therefore modeled as probable contextual links.

The *Psalms of Solomon* (c. 70–40 BCE, probably Pharisaic in origin) are 18 psalms preserved in Greek and Syriac, not attributed to Solomon in the oldest manuscripts. They describe the Hasmonean rulers as wicked usurpers and celebrate the Roman conquest of Jerusalem (63 BCE, Pompey) as divine judgment, then lament Pompey's death (48 BCE) as further judgment. Key messianic content: Ps. Sol. 17–18 contain the most detailed pre-Christian Jewish messianic expectation — a Davidic king who will purge Jerusalem of Gentiles, rule in righteousness, and gather the dispersed of Israel. The Messiah is called 'Lord Messiah' (*kyrios christos*, Ps. Sol. 17:32) — a direct terminological parallel to NT usage. Relevance to this dataset: the Psalms of Solomon provide the closest Jewish parallel to early Christian messianic expectation and demonstrate that 'Christ/Messiah' as a title for a coming Davidic ruler was well established in Palestinian Judaism before Jesus. In this dataset, Psalms of Solomon passages are cited as `contextualizes` evidence for messianic claims.

The Quartodeciman controversy (c. 190–195 CE) pitted [[person:victor-i-of-rome|Victor I]] of Rome, who demanded all churches celebrate Easter on the Sunday after Passover, against the Asian churches led by [[person:polycrates-of-ephesus|Polycrates of Ephesus]], who maintained the tradition of celebrating on 14 Nisan (hence 'Quartodeciman' = fourteenth). [[person:irenaeus-of-lyons|Irenaeus]] mediated, arguing diversity on this point had never broken communion (Eusebius HE 5.23–25). Victor threatened excommunication; it is debated whether he actually carried this out. The Polycarp-Anicetus precedent (c. 155 CE) established that peaceful disagreement was possible. The controversy is foundational for understanding early episcopal authority and its limits.

Irenaeus's role in the Quartodeciman controversy is fully attested by Eusebius HE 5.24, which preserves a summary of Irenaeus's letter to Victor urging peace. Irenaeus's argument was not to adjudicate which side was right but to insist that diversity on this point had never broken ecclesial unity — citing Polycarp's own visit to Anicetus as precedent. The participant_in claim is therefore attested with a mediator rather than partisan role.

The authorship of Revelation is disputed. The author identifies himself as 'John' (Rev 1:1, 1:9, 22:8) writing from Patmos, but ancient sources debate whether this is John the Apostle (Irenaeus AH 5.30, Justin Dial. 81), 'the Elder John' (Papias, as argued by Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius HE 7.25), or another John entirely. Dionysius of Alexandria conducted the first critical stylistic comparison with the Gospel of John and concluded they were by different authors. The date is also disputed: Domitian (c. 95 CE, majority view) vs. Nero (c. 68 CE, based on internal evidence). Claims about Revelation's authorship are modeled as `claimed_tradition` for the apostolic attribution.

The Roman episcopal succession list is attested in multiple 2nd–3rd century sources with some variation: Hegesippus (c. 165 CE, quoted in Eusebius HE 4.22), Irenaeus (*AH* 3.3.3, c. 180 CE), and Eusebius (*HE* 3.2, 4–15, c. 313 CE). The standard list: Peter → Linus → Anacletus/Anencletus → Clement → Evaristus → Alexander I → Sixtus I → Telesphorus → Hyginus → Pius I → Anicetus → Soter → Eleutherius → Victor → Zephyrinus → Callistus → Urban → Pontian → Anterus → Fabian → Cornelius → Lucius → Stephen → Sixtus II → Dionysius → Felix I → Eutychianus → Caius → Marcellinus. The earliest figures (Linus through Clement) are disputed as to whether they represent monarchical bishops or leading elders. The `bishop_of` predicate for these early figures carries `probable` certainty reflecting this ambiguity. From Victor I (c. 189–199 CE) onward, the episcopal office is clearly monarchical. See also `note-clement-bishop-precision` and `note-clement-rome-episcopal`.

Romans (c. 56–58 CE, from Corinth) is Paul's most systematic theological letter — often described as his magnum opus. Structure: (1) 1–4: righteousness of God, human sinfulness, justification by faith; (2) 5–8: life in Christ, the Spirit, future glory; (3) 9–11: Israel and salvation history ('the mystery of Israel'); (4) 12–16: practical ethics, community relations. Unusual character: unlike Paul's other letters, Romans was not written to a community Paul founded. He wrote in preparation for his planned visit (Rom 15:24), possibly to secure support for a mission to Spain, and possibly to mediate Jewish-Gentile tensions in the Roman house churches. Authorship is `attested` — universally accepted, one of the seven undisputed Pauline letters (with 1–2 Cor, Gal, Phil, 1 Thess, Phlm). The letter cites Phoebe as a *diakonos* of Cenchreae (16:1) — key evidence for women in ministry leadership in early Christianity.

The *regula fidei* ('rule of faith') is the pre-creedal summary of Christian doctrine used as a hermeneutical norm in 2nd–3rd century theology. Key witnesses: (1) Irenaeus (*AH* 1.10.1): trinitarian structure — one God who made all things; Christ Jesus who became flesh; the Holy Spirit who through the prophets proclaimed the divine economy; (2) Tertullian (*De Praes.* 13; *De Virg. Vel.* 1): similar trinitarian summary, used to adjudicate appeals to Scripture against heretics; (3) Origen (*De Princ.* Preface): identifies the 'ecclesiastical preaching' as the fixed deposit distinct from speculative theology. The *regula* differs from the later creeds in: being narrative and doxological rather than propositional; varying in exact wording between authors; functioning as an interpretive key rather than a legal formula. Relationship to canon and creed: the *regula* is chronologically prior to the fixed NT canon and the developed creeds, showing that doctrinal consensus preceded textual canonization. In this dataset, claims about the *regula fidei* content are modeled as `work_affirms_proposition` linked to the relevant patristic work.
Saturninus taught the Saviour was unborn, incorporeal, and only appeared human — classically docetist. His membership in the broader docetist movement is modeled as probable.

Seed dataset is intentionally limited to the public ministry of [[person:jesus-of-nazareth]]. Places like [[place:galilee]] and [[place:jerusalem]] are included only insofar as they are needed for ministry-period claims.

Primary evidence in this starter set is weighted toward the canonical Gospels. [[work:antiquities-of-the-jews|Josephus's Antiquities]] is included as a contextual non-Christian witness for [[person:john-the-baptist]] and [[person:pontius-pilate]].

The Shapurian persecution under Shapur II (337–379 CE) was directed primarily at Persian Christians in the Sasanid Empire, coinciding with Constantine I's Christianization of the Roman Empire. Shapur II regarded his empire's Christians as potential Roman sympathizers and imposed heavy taxes, then outright persecution. The Syriac *Acts of the Persian Martyrs* (Bedjan edition) document the execution of thousands of Persian Christians, including bishops, priests, and lay people. [[person:aphrahat|Aphrahat the Persian Sage]] wrote his *Demonstrations* (337–345 CE) during this persecution, addressing communities under severe pressure. The *fall-of-nisibis* event (363 CE, ceded to Persia by Jovian after Julian's defeat) is related context: [[person:ephrem-the-syrian|Ephrem]] fled Nisibis at this point, settling in Edessa for the final decade of his life. Year claims for Persian martyrdom events carry `probable` certainty reflecting the limited precision of Syriac martyrology dating.

The *Shepherd of Hermas* (c. 100–160 CE) occupied a unique position in the early church: widely read and highly regarded, it appears in the Codex Sinaiticus after Revelation, suggesting full canonical status in some communities. The Muratorian Fragment (c. 170–200 CE, probably Roman) accepts Hermas's spiritual value but excludes it from public reading — because it was written 'recently' by Hermas, brother of Bishop Pius I of Rome. Origen (*Comm. Rom.* 10.31) cites it as Scripture. Eusebius (*HE* 3.3.6) classifies it as *notha* (spurious). Athanasius (*Festal Letter* 39, 367 CE) lists it as useful for instruction but not canonical. The Hermas debate illustrates the fluidity of canonical boundaries before the 4th century. In this dataset, proposition claims derived from Hermas are modeled as `work_affirms_proposition` rather than treated as Scripture, following the modern scholarly convention.

The *Shepherd of Hermas* (c. 100–155 CE, Rome) is the longest of the Apostolic Fathers and was extremely popular in the early church, treated as canonical by some (Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen). Structure: Five Visions, Twelve Mandates, Ten Similitudes. Authorship: the Muratorian Fragment identifies the author as 'Hermas, brother of Pius, bishop of Rome' (c. 140–154 CE) — but internal tradition claims a Clement of Rome connection. Likely composed in stages c. 100–155 CE. Theological distinctives: (1) Second repentance — one post-baptismal repentance opportunity for the 'lapsed'; central for penitential theology; (2) Angelology — the 'Shepherd' is the angel of repentance; (3) Christology is fluid/unclear (Spirit-Christology? Angel-Christology?); (4) The church as a tower being built from living stones. Significance: primary evidence for Rome's theology of penance c. 100–150 CE; popular with catechumens; status as canonical eventually declined when the canon was formally settled. In this dataset, Hermas serves as evidence for Roman Christian theology and practice in the early-mid 2nd century.

Syriac Christianity (centered on Edessa/Osrhoene) represents one of the earliest and most distinctive branches of early Christianity, developing independently of the Greek-speaking Mediterranean tradition. Key features: (1) Syriac (eastern Aramaic) as liturgical language, closely related to Jesus's own Aramaic dialect; (2) Tatian's *Diatessaron* (gospel harmony) was the standard Gospel text in Syriac churches until the 5th century; (3) Distinct christological vocabulary (*shem*, *ruha*) and ascetic tradition; (4) [[person:ephrem-the-syrian|Ephrem the Syrian]] (c. 306–373 CE) represents the classical Syriac tradition at its height; (5) Bardaisan of Edessa shows that early Edessene Christianity was theologically diverse before orthodox consolidation. The Syriac tradition's relationship to Mesopotamian Jewish Christianity and to Thomas Christianity makes it essential context for understanding eastward Christian expansion.

The Peshitta (from Syriac *pešîttā*, 'simple/common') is the standard version of the Christian Bible in Syriac, serving a role analogous to the Latin Vulgate in Western Christianity. The OT Peshitta was translated from Hebrew, largely pre-Christian, possibly by the Jewish community of Adiabene; some books may have been translated by Jewish Christians. The NT Peshitta's origins are complex: (1) Tatian's *Diatessaron* was the standard Gospel text in Syriac Christianity until the 5th century; (2) The four separate Gospels in the Peshitta were introduced by Rabbula, bishop of Edessa (d. 435 CE), replacing the Diatessaron; (3) The Peshitta NT contains only 22 books — it lacks 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, and Revelation (which remain outside the Syriac canon in many communities). Claims in this dataset about Syriac Christianity's Scripture use should note the Diatessaron-Peshitta transition and the narrower Syriac NT canon.

Tacitus's *Annals* 15.44 (written c. 116–120 CE) is one of the two most important pagan references to Jesus and early Christianity. The passage: 'Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus, and a most mischievous superstition, thus checked for the moment, again broke out not only in Judaea, the first source of the evil, but even in Rome.' Significance: (1) Independent Roman confirmation of Jesus's execution under Pilate; (2) Locates early Christian expansion in both Judaea and Rome by Nero's time (64 CE); (3) The term 'superstition' (*superstitio*) is technically negative — Tacitus clearly does not sympathize with Christians. Authenticity: accepted by virtually all historians; the interpolation theory (Hochart, Price) has minimal scholarly support. The passage's value for this dataset: confirms the Neronian persecution context and the Roman Christian community by 64 CE.

[[person:tacitus|Tacitus]] (c. 56–120 CE) is the most important Roman historian for early Christian history.
