His two major works: - *Annals* (c. 116–120 CE): covers Tiberius through Nero; includes the famous passage on Nero's persecution of Christians (15.44); - *Histories* (c. 100–110 CE): covers 69–96 CE; includes a hostile ethnography of Jews in Book 5. His authorship is inferred from: Pliny the Younger's correspondence (9 letters to 'Tacitus'); explicit self-identification in *Agricola* and *Germania*; stylistic continuity across all works. Value as a source: Tacitus had access to senatorial archives and official records; he is explicitly hostile to Christians (*exitiabilis superstitio*, 'a destructive superstition') and to Jews, making his attestations to the Christian origins in Judaea all the more significant as external, non-sympathetic confirmation. In this dataset, Tacitus's works are used as `contextualizes` or `supports` evidence where they explicitly name events, places, or persons.

[[person:tatian-the-assyrian|Tatian]] (c. 120–c. 180 CE) was an Assyrian apologist and theologian, student of Justin Martyr, and founder of the Encratite sect. **The Diatessaron**: Tatian's most influential work was a harmony of the four Gospels (*Diatessaron* = 'through four') composed c. 170 CE; likely written in Syriac for the Eastern church. It was the standard Gospel text in Syriac Christianity until replaced by the separate Gospels in the 5th century (Theodoret of Cyrrhus reportedly destroyed 200 copies). The Diatessaron is known through: secondary quotations; the *Commentarius* of Ephrem the Syrian; an Arabic translation; and a Latin excerpt (*Codex Fuldensis*). **Oration to the Greeks**: Tatian's surviving apologetic work attacks Greek philosophy and culture as inferior to 'barbarian' (i.e., biblical) wisdom; provides early testimony on idol worship and demonology. **Encratism**: After Justin's martyrdom, Tatian returned to Syria and founded the Encratites, who rejected marriage, meat, and wine (using water in the Eucharist — *Aquarii*). Eusebius *HE* 4.29 describes this development. **Dataset note**: Claims cover his affirmation of the Gospel harmony (Diatessaron) and encratite teaching, evidenced by Tertullian and Eusebius.
After Justin's death Tatian returned East. The Diatessaron's Syriac composition localizes him at Edessa.

Tatian mentions in Oration 29 that he studied under an unnamed teacher whose teachings changed his life; patristic tradition (Irenaeus AH 1.28.1, Eusebius HE 4.29) identifies this as Justin Martyr. Tatian's Oration reflects close theological dependence on Justin's Logos theology and apologist method. The teacher_of claim is modeled as attested (not merely probable) because Irenaeus explicitly names the connection.

The term 'catholic church' (*hē katholikē ekklēsia*, the universal/whole church) first appears in [[person:ignatius-of-antioch|Ignatius of Antioch]] (*Smyrn.* 8.2, c. 107–117 CE): 'Wherever the bishop appears, there let the congregation be, just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church.' The term means 'universal' or 'whole' — the church that includes all Christians everywhere, as distinguished from local congregations. In Ignatius, the term is not yet polemically used (it does not distinguish orthodoxy from heresy); it simply affirms the unity of the whole body gathered under the bishop. The polemical use — 'catholic' as 'orthodox' vs. 'heretical' — develops through the Quartodeciman controversy and against Marcionism. By the 3rd century, 'Catholic church' had become the standard self-designation of the proto-orthodox mainstream over against schismatic and heretical groups.

The term 'Christian' (*Christianos*) first appears in Acts 11:26: 'the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.' This is the earliest textual attestation of the label, dated c. 40–50 CE within the narrative. Pliny the Younger (*Ep.* 10.96, c. 112 CE) uses it as an established self-designation among the accused. Tacitus (*Ann.* 15.44, written c. 117 CE) identifies Christians as followers of 'Christus' executed under Pilate. The term was likely coined by outsiders (as a gentile nickname for 'Messiah-people') before being adopted by believers. Ignatius (*Ign. Magn.* 10, *Ign. Rom.* 3, *Ign. Eph.* 11) is the first Christian writer to use the term self-consciously as a positive identity marker: 'it is not my business to only be called a Christian, but also to be one.' Claims in this dataset that use 'Christian' as a descriptor reflect this established usage by the time of our earliest sources.

Tertullian's *Apologeticum* (c. 197 CE) is the most systematic and rhetorically sophisticated 2nd-century defense of Christianity to pagan authorities. Addressed formally to Roman provincial governors, it argues: (1) Christians are innocent of the three main charges: atheism, treason, immorality; (2) Roman law's procedure against Christians is unjust — the name alone is punished; (3) Christianity surpasses Roman religion in morality and philosophical coherence; (4) The famous reversal: 'The blood of Christians is seed' (*Apol.* 50.13), often misquoted as 'The blood of martyrs is the seed of the church.' The *Apologeticum* is the primary Latin source for: 2nd-century Christian worship practices (ch. 39 — the weekly assembly, love feast, Scripture reading, prayer), Christian ethics, and the theology of martyrdom as witness. Its relationship to earlier Greek apologists (Athenagoras, Justin) is debated — Tertullian may have known Justin's *Apology* but the dependence is not direct.

[[work:de-baptismo|Tertullian's *De Baptismo*]] (c. 200–206 CE) is the earliest surviving Christian treatise exclusively on baptism. Key positions: (1) Baptism is necessary for salvation but not magically efficacious — it requires appropriate repentance and faith. (2) The formula is trinitarian (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), citing Matthew 28:19. (3) Tertullian argues against infant baptism (ch. 18) — 'Why, indeed, is it necessary... that the sponsors likewise should be thrust into danger?' — the earliest extant argument against the practice, and the only pre-Nicene anti-paedobaptist statement from a major author. (4) He defends the validity of water baptism against Quintilla's group (who rejected the material rite). The work is also the primary source for 2nd–3rd century baptismal liturgy: anointing, hand-laying, milk-and-honey, weekly celebrations of the resurrection. Its pre-Montanist authorship is generally accepted; Tertullian's later Montanist writings take a stricter position on baptism's moral demands.

[[work:de-carne-christi|Tertullian's *De Carne Christi*]] (c. 210 CE) is the most systematic early Christian defense of the physical reality of the incarnation against Docetist and Marcionite positions. The famous anti-Docetist slogan 'credo quia absurdum' (I believe because it is absurd) does not actually appear in the text in that form; the actual statement (ch. 5) is: 'And the Son of God died; it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd.' The work is also the primary Latin source for the Valentinian and Marcionite positions on Christ's body, making it essential for understanding 2nd–3rd century christological debates. Proposition claims about Christ's physical birth and physical resurrection (*De Resurr. Carnis*) draw heavily on Tertullian's anti-Docetist corpus.

[[person:tertullian|Tertullian]] joined the New Prophecy (Montanist) movement c. 207–213 CE, after which his works show increasingly rigorist positions on second marriage, flight from persecution, military service, and the authority of the Paraclete's new revelations over ecclesiastical hierarchy. Works written in his Montanist period include *De Monogamia*, *De Ieiunio*, *De Fuga*, and *De Pudicitia*. His earlier apologetic and theological works (*Apologeticum*, *Adv. Marcionem*, *Adv. Praxean*, *De Baptismo*, *De Praescriptione*) are broadly catholic. The chronology is debated; Tertullian may never have formally joined an organized Montanist sect but rather developed his own independent rigorist position. Proposition claims from his Montanist works are flagged with this context where relevant.

[[person:tertullian|Tertullian]] (c. 155–c. 240 CE) is the father of Latin theology and one of the most prolific early Christian writers. **Phases**: - *Orthodox phase* (c. 196–207): defends Christianity against pagans (*Apologeticum*), against heretics (*De Praescriptione*, *Adversus Marcionem*, *Adversus Praxean*), and writes on discipline (*De Baptismo*, *De Oratione*); - *Montanist phase* (c. 207–212+): joins the New Prophecy movement; writes polemics against the institutional church (*De Ieiunio*, *De Monogamia*, *De Pudicitia*). **Theological contributions**: - Coined or fixed key Latin theological vocabulary: *trinitas*, *persona*, *substantia*, *satisfactio*, *sacramentum*; - Developed the rule of faith (*regula fidei*) as hermeneutical principle; - Articulated the doctrine of two natures in Christ (*Adversus Praxean*). **Controversies**: His Montanist phase and rigorist ethics (opposing second marriage, theatrical shows, military service) make his relationship to mainstream orthodoxy complex. Jerome (*De Viris Ill.* 53) says he 'fell away from the church on account of the envy and abuse of the Roman clergy.' **Dataset note**: Multiple Tertullian claims in this dataset cover his Carthaginian origins, Trinitarian formula, catechumenate, fasting, and Montanist membership.

Tertullian's list of nations who have come to faith in Christ ([[work:adversus-judaeos-tertullian|Adv. Jud.]] 7) is a rhetorical flourish arguing for the fulfillment of Psalm 2 and Isaiah 45. The list includes Parthians, Medes, Elamites, British, Moors, and others. It should not be read as documentary evidence of organized Christian communities in each named region; rather it attests Tertullian's *claim* that Christianity had reached these areas. The claims based on this passage are tagged `claimed_tradition` or `contextualizes` rather than `supports` for specific regional presence.

[[person:theophilus-of-antioch|Theophilus of Antioch]] (bishop c. 169–183 CE) is notable for several 'firsts' in Christian literature: (1) First Christian author to use the word *Trias* (Trinity) for the Father, Word, and Wisdom (*Ad Autolycum* 2.15); (2) *Ad Autolycum* is the earliest surviving complete Christian apologetic work in Greek addressed to a named pagan; (3) He demonstrates detailed engagement with Greek philosophical tradition while insisting on the superiority of Hebrew chronology and Scripture. His trinitarian formula distinguishes him from later binitarian apologists: Theophilus explicitly includes the Holy Spirit in the divine triad. The claim `clm-ad-autolycum-affirms-trinity` is modeled as `attested` with high confidence based on *Ad Autolycum* 2.15.

[[work:ad-autolycum]] 2.15 contains the first known Christian use of the Greek term Τριάς (Trinity), applied to God, his Word, and his Wisdom. This is significant enough to warrant the editorial note. The Logos proposition claimed (logos-is-pre-existent-son-of-god) is a fit because Theophilus explicitly describes the Logos as begotten from God before creation. The Trinity term itself is not captured as a separate proposition but is contextually significant for the Logos claim.

3 John (the shortest NT book at 219 Greek words) is a personal letter from 'the Elder' to Gaius, praising his hospitality to traveling missionaries and criticizing Diotrephes 'who loves to be first' and refuses to receive the Elder's messengers. Historical significance: 3 John provides a rare glimpse of conflict between itinerant charismatic authority (the Elder) and local episcopal authority (Diotrephes). The conflict illuminates the transition from apostolic/prophetic to monarchical-episcopal governance. Authorship: same 'Elder' as 2 John; traditionally John the Apostle, but may be a distinct Elder John (Papias's testimony, Eusebius HE 3.39). Diotrephes: sometimes read as a proto-Gnostic or simply as an independent-minded local bishop. The text does not specify his theology. Demetrius is commended — possibly the letter-carrier. Canonical status: among the *antilegomena* of Eusebius (HE 3.25.3); included in Athanasius's canon (367 CE). In this dataset, 3 John is used as evidence for early church governance conflicts and the authority of 'the Elder.'

The claim that [[person:thomas|Thomas the Apostle]] preached in India rests on the [[work:acts-of-thomas|Acts of Thomas]] (c. 220-240 CE) and later church tradition preserved in [[work:rufinus-ecclesiastical-history|Rufinus]] and [[work:ecclesiastical-history-of-eusebius|Eusebius]]. The Acts of Thomas is a Syriac apocryphal work composed long after the events it purports to describe. Mainstream scholarship treats the India mission as legendary, though the 'Thomas Christians' of India (Nasrani) trace their origin to this tradition. Claims based on this evidence are tagged `claimed_tradition` rather than `attested`.

Valentinus (c. 100–160 CE) founded the most influential Gnostic school of the 2nd century. Educated at Alexandria, he came to Rome c. 136 CE and reportedly came close to being elected bishop (Tertullian *Adv. Val.* 4). His system: a complex divine Pleroma of 30 Aeons arranged in syzygies (male-female pairs), from which the Demiurge (a lower deity, not the highest God) created the material world. Humans contain divine sparks that must ascend back to the Pleroma through Gnosis. Primary sources: fragments preserved in Clement of Alexandria (*Strom.*) and Hippolytus (*Ref.* 6.29–37); the *Gospel of Truth* (Nag Hammadi I.3 and XII.2) is possibly by Valentinus himself. His school split into Eastern (Theodotus) and Western (Ptolemy, Heracleon) branches after his death. Irenaeus (*AH* 1.1–8) provides the fullest account of Ptolemaic Valentinianism. Irenaeus's *Against Heresies* was written specifically against Valentinianism (Ptolemy's school, in Lyon) — making Valentinus the polemical center of 2nd-century anti-Gnostic literature. In this dataset, Valentinian theological claims use `probable` certainty and `strong_inference` mode where only Irenaeus's secondary account survives.

[[person:valentinus|Valentinus]] (c. 100–160 CE) was the most sophisticated Gnostic theologian of the 2nd century, active in Rome c. 136–165 CE. According to Tertullian (*Adv. Val.* 4), he was a candidate for bishop of Rome but lost the election to a confessor, precipitating his move toward heterodoxy. This account is from a hostile source and should be treated cautiously. Valentinus's own writings survive only in fragments: the *Gospel of Truth* (from Nag Hammadi, NH I.3) is attributed to Valentinus by Irenaeus (AH 3.11.9), though this identification is debated. His system: a complex Pleroma of 30 Aeons, the Fall of Sophia, the Demiurge, and three classes of humans (pneumatic, psychic, hylic). His pupils Ptolemy and Heracleon systematized 'Eastern' Valentinianism; Marcus (of the Marcosians) is a distinct offshoot. The `active_in=rome` claim is `attested` based on explicit statement in Irenaeus AH 3.4.3 and Tertullian.

The Valerian persecution (257–260 CE) specifically targeted Christian clergy and prohibited assemblies at cemeteries. Edict I (257 CE) required clergy to perform state cult sacrifice; Edict II (258 CE) mandated execution of bishops, priests, and deacons. [[person:cyprian-of-carthage|Cyprian]] was martyred on 14 September 258 CE under Proconsul Galerius Maximus — the first bishop of Carthage to be martyred. The *Acta Proconsularia Cypriani* preserve the trial transcript. This is one of the most precisely documented early Christian martyrdoms: day, month, year, and the official record all survive. The `cyprians-martyrdom` event year 258 CE is therefore `attested` with high confidence.

The *Wisdom of Solomon* (c. 100 BCE–50 CE, Alexandria, Greek) is a deuterocanonical/apocryphal text that is canonical in Catholic and Orthodox traditions but not in Protestant or Jewish canons. Author: Pseudonymously Solomon; actually an Alexandrian Jewish author writing sophisticated Greek (likely c. 30 BCE–10 CE based on literary and historical allusions). Key themes: (1) The fate of the righteous and wicked in afterlife (Wis 3:1–9: 'the souls of the righteous are in God's hands'); (2) Wisdom as a divine hypostasis — a female personification who participates in creation; (3) Anti-idolatry polemic (Wis 13–15). NT connections: Wis 7:25–26 on Wisdom's attributes influenced Heb 1:3 and Col 1:15 (Christ as image and radiance of God); Wis 2:12–20 ('if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him') may lie behind Mt 27:43's mockery of Jesus on the cross. In this dataset, Wisdom of Solomon passages are cited as contextual background for early Christian Christological development.

The role of women in early Christianity is among the most debated questions in NT and patristic scholarship. Key evidence clusters: (1) *Pauline letters*: Phoebe — *diakonos* and *prostatis* (Rom 16:1–2); Prisca/Priscilla — Paul's co-worker (*synergos*, Rom 16:3); Junia — 'outstanding among the apostles' (Rom 16:7); Philip's prophesying daughters (Acts 21:9). (2) *Corinthian correspondence*: women prophesy (1 Cor 11:5); the silence command (1 Cor 14:34–35) may be a later interpolation (Payne, Allison) or addressed to a specific disruptive behavior. (3) *Pastoral Epistles* (later): 1 Tim 2:12 ('I do not permit a woman to teach or have authority') — most restrictive; reflects later consolidation. (4) *Pliny Ep.* 10.96: *ministrae* = deaconesses (early 2nd century, Bithynia). (5) *Didascalia* (c. 230–250 CE): explicit deaconess office. (6) Montanism: Prisca and Maximilla as prophets; the New Prophecy explicitly endorsed female prophetic leadership. The trajectory: egalitarian house-church practice → gradual institutionalization → restriction of women to deaconess role (mainly serving women) → exclusion from presbyterate by c. 300 CE.
